title: Tags, releases and branching strategies
summary: Tag what you ship, version it meaningfully, and choose between trunk-based development and GitFlow.

steps.title: Tags
body: A **tag** is a ref that never moves: a permanent name for the commit you released.
```text
git tag -a v1.4.0 -m "Release 1.4.0"   # annotated: its own object with tagger, date, message (use for releases)
git tag v1.4.0-rc1                     # lightweight: just a name, like a branch that never moves
git push origin v1.4.0                 # tags are NOT pushed by plain git push
git push --follow-tags                 # push commits plus the annotated tags pointing at them
git switch --detach v1.4.0             # look at exactly what shipped
Platforms turn a pushed tag into a **release** with notes and build artifacts, and CI pipelines often deploy on tag push.
Never move a published tag. If 1.4.0 was wrong, ship 1.4.1: anyone who already fetched v1.4.0 keeps the old meaning.

steps.prompt: You run `git tag -a v2.0.0 -m "2.0"` and then `git push`. Your colleague does `git fetch` and cannot see the tag. Why?
options: Plain `git push` does not push tags; run `git push origin v2.0.0` or `git push --follow-tags`
steps.explain: Branches and tags are pushed separately. Teams often set `git config --global push.followTags true`.

steps.title: Semantic versioning
body: `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, for example `2.7.3`:
| Bump | When | Example |
| PATCH | backwards-compatible bug fix | 2.7.3 -> 2.7.4 |
| MINOR | new feature, backwards compatible | 2.7.3 -> 2.8.0 |
| MAJOR | breaking change | 2.7.3 -> 3.0.0 |
Lower numbers reset to 0 when a higher one bumps.

**Conventional Commits** make the bump automatic by prefixing subjects: `fix: ...`, `feat: ...`, and `feat!: ...` or a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer for breaking ones. Tools read the commits since the last tag and compute the next version and changelog.

steps.prompt: The last release is `v1.4.2`. Since then these commits landed. What is the next version? (Like `v1.5.0`.)
steps.explain: There is a `feat`, so MINOR bumps and PATCH resets. No breaking change, so MAJOR stays.

steps.prompt: Which part of the version bumps?
items: Fix a null reference in checkout
Correct a typo in an error message

steps.title: Branching strategies
body: **Trunk-based development** (most modern teams):
```text
main  ---o---o---o---o---o---o---o---   always releasable, deployed often
short-lived branches (hours to 2 days), merged via PR
Unfinished features are hidden behind **feature flags**, not long branches. Releases are tags on `main` (or short release branches cut from it for hotfixes).
**GitFlow** (versioned products with slow, scheduled releases):
```text
main      ---o-----------------o-------   only released versions, tagged
develop   ---o---o---o---o---o---o---o-   integration branch
feature/*        \---o---o---/
release/*                  \---o---/      stabilise, then merge to main + develop
hotfix/*  branch from main, merge to main + develop

GitFlow costs more merging and longer-lived branches (bigger conflicts). Trunk-based needs good CI, tests and feature flags. Pick trunk-based unless you really must support several released versions at once.

steps.prompt: Match each practice to the problem it solves.
pairs: ship unfinished work to `main` without exposing it
integrate features before a scheduled release
the fix reaches both the release and future work
Branches that live a day or two
small PRs and few merge conflicts

steps.prompt: Your team deploys a web app to production several times a day. Which strategy fits best?
options: Trunk-based: short-lived branches into `main`, feature flags, tag or deploy from `main`
One branch per developer, merged every quarter
No branches; everyone commits to `main` without review
steps.explain: Continuous delivery needs `main` always releasable and small changes. GitFlow's release branches add delay you do not need.

steps.title: Next version from commits
prompt: > Release tools such as release-please and semantic-release make this decision from the commit log. Write the core rule yourself once, so you know exactly what they will decide; the next step then tags a release with real Git.
Write `NextVersion(string current, List<string> subjects)` for Conventional Commits:
- **Breaking** if any subject contains `BREAKING CHANGE`, or its type (the part before the first `:`) ends with `!` (like `feat!:` or `fix(api)!:`). Then `v<major+1>.0.0`.
- Else if any subject starts with `feat`: `v<major>.<minor+1>.0`.
- Else if any subject starts with `fix`: bump patch.
starter: static string NextVersion(string current, List<string> subjects)
solution: static string NextVersion(string current, List<string> subjects)
int major = parts[0], minor = parts[1], patch = parts[2];
bool breaking = subjects.Any(s => s.Contains("BREAKING CHANGE") || s.Split(':')[0].EndsWith("!"));
hints: Check breaking first, then feat, then fix.
template: Dojo.Eq("feat bumps minor", "v1.5.0", NextVersion("v1.4.2", new() { "fix: handle empty cart", "feat: add gift cards" }));
Dojo.Eq("fix bumps patch", "v1.4.3", NextVersion("v1.4.2", new() { "fix: round VAT" }));
Dojo.Eq("! means breaking", "v2.0.0", NextVersion("v1.4.2", new() { "feat!: drop v1 API" }));
Dojo.Eq("scoped breaking", "v2.0.0", NextVersion("v1.4.2", new() { "fix(api)!: change error shape" }));
Dojo.Eq("BREAKING CHANGE text", "v4.0.0", NextVersion("v3.9.9", new() { "refactor: new config BREAKING CHANGE" }));
Dojo.Eq("docs only: no release", "v1.4.2", NextVersion("v1.4.2", new() { "docs: readme", "chore: bump deps" }));

steps.title: Tag the release, remove a wrong tag
prompt: `main` in `~/shop` is ready for release 1.5.0, and pushed.
1. Create an **annotated** tag `v1.5.0` on `main` with the message `Release 1.5.0`, and push that one tag.
2. Someone pushed a tag `v1.5.0-rc` on the wrong commit. Delete it on the server **and** locally.

checks.name: the server has an annotated v1.5.0 on main
checks.cmd: test "$(git -C /srv/git/shop.git cat-file -t v1.5.0)" = tag && test "$(git -C /srv/git/shop.git rev-parse 'v1.5.0^{commit}')" = "$(git -C /srv/git/shop.git rev-parse main)"
checks.fail: The server should have `v1.5.0` as an annotated tag (`-a`) pointing at `main`. Tags are not pushed by plain `git push`: `git push origin v1.5.0`.

checks.name: v1.5.0-rc is gone everywhere
checks.cmd: ! git -C /srv/git/shop.git rev-parse -q --verify refs/tags/v1.5.0-rc && cd ~/shop && ! git rev-parse -q --verify refs/tags/v1.5.0-rc
checks.fail: `v1.5.0-rc` still exists. `git push origin --delete v1.5.0-rc` removes it on the server, `git tag -d v1.5.0-rc` locally.

hints: `git tag -a v1.5.0 -m "Release 1.5.0"` tags the commit you are on.
`git push origin v1.5.0` pushes one tag (avoid `--tags`: it pushes every local tag, including experiments).
`git push origin --delete v1.5.0-rc` and `git tag -d v1.5.0-rc`.
steps.explain: Annotated tags are real objects with a tagger, a date and a message (and they can be signed with `-s`); `git describe` uses them. Deleting a pushed tag is easy on the server but clones that already fetched it keep it, so never re-use a release tag for different code: tag a new version instead.
